source.title: Scaling Multilingual Mixture-of-Experts: How Language Coverage Changes Capacity and Compute Allocation
source.authors: Joel Dag; Nikit Srivastava; Hamada M. Zahera; Axel-Cyrille Ngonga Ngomo

record.file_problem: The text is substantially complete. Some equations and figure/table layouts are flattened or garbled, but the relevant numerical results and narrative descriptions are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures per-language validation loss across a controlled grid of multilingual MoE sizes, expert counts, training horizons, and language coverage, and evaluates fitted scaling-law predictions on held-out configurations. This is a different setting and formulation from the original dense-model scaling studies.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own loss measurements, scaling-law fits and held-out prediction errors, capacity-allocation comparisons, and downstream evaluations. Cited scaling-law results are not recorded as findings. Routing diagnostics are not included because they measure routing patterns rather than the claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study fits power-law loss laws in a new setting: multilingual decoder-only Top-1 MoEs across 64 configurations with N, Dt, E and K varied. It reports its own held-out and larger-model prediction errors, which bear on V1, V2, V5 and V7. The method is ordinary power-law fitting of held-out loss, so T3 (new setting) fits better than T2. Its allocation analysis splits active parameters against experts under total-parameter budgets, not parameters against tokens, so it does not test V3.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that multilingual MoE scaling is a joint allocation problem over active parameters, experts, tokens per language and coverage. In their data, 32 experts cut the 12→200-language loss penalty by 83% at matched tokens per language. Their repetition-aware law cuts held-out error 28% versus JointMoE (Dt), and repetition terms matter for extrapolating to longer runs. Restoring mean loss after expansion leaves 32 of 50 languages worse off.
record.recipe_differences: The study develops a repetition-aware joint loss law for multilingual Top-1 MoEs, adds language coverage, expert count, and per-language effective exposure, and evaluates predictions on a controlled multilingual grid rather than reproducing either original dense-model setup.
record.method_sensitivity: Prediction errors and allocation choices vary with the scaling-law formulation, expert and coverage parameterizations, treatment of repeated data, and parameter count used in the repetition discount. Coverage-composition comparisons also use interpolation choices; the authors report that the main expert-coverage direction persists across tested interpolation methods. The learning-rate check reports that its prescribed rule outperforms a fixed rate in all nine tested configurations.

fits_no_version.finding: Expert count reduces the matched-Dt loss penalty of expanding from K=12 to K=200, from 0.0796 at E=1 to 0.0135 at E=32. The reduction is 66–84% across three seeds.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In multilingual MoEs, added experts reduce the per-language loss cost of broader language coverage.

fits_no_version.finding: Broader language coverage delays the switch from expert-heavy to active-heavy configurations under a fixed total-parameter budget. The observed delay is 1.62x (0.4B budget); the predicted delay is 2.70x (5.1B budget).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The preferred split between active and expert capacity under a fixed total-parameter budget shifts toward experts as language coverage grows.

fits_no_version.finding: Expert gains differ by coverage on downstream and likelihood benchmarks. They are larger at K=200 on MultiBLiMP, FLORES and NTREX, and smaller at K=200 on HellaSwag and XStoryCloze.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The expert × coverage loss interaction transfers to external likelihood, but its downstream accuracy effect depends on the task.

record.problems: The main factorial grid uses one seed; additional seeds cover selected settings only. The evidence is restricted to decoder-only Top-1 MoEs, fixed tokenizer and corpus, and E ≤ 32. The held-out tests exclude configurations on grid axes but use target languages represented during fitting. The larger-model stress test is one setting. Allocation uses logical FLOPs and excludes hardware overheads, which the authors report separately. Several figure/table passages are flattened in the supplied text.
record.rows_left_out: The full per-configuration benchmark scores in Appendix F, Table 21, and the many per-language/per-size loss and allocation curves are not extracted individually; the response records the paper's explicit aggregate benchmark findings and principal allocation results instead. Routing diagnostics in Appendix G and detailed physical-cost comparisons in Appendix H do not directly measure a listed claim version.

untested.parts: Single-variable laws over several orders of magnitude (N spans only 93M to 590M); dense text-only models.
Extrapolation by orders of magnitude; tested only about 1.7–2x beyond the fitted grid.
Entire version: no compute-optimal parameter-versus-token allocation is estimated.
Entire version: depth and width co-vary with N and are never varied at fixed N.
Image and video modalities, fine-tuning, and transfer. Only repeated data in multilingual text pretraining is tested.
Any fitted mapping from scale or loss to downstream accuracy.
Fitted exponents and how they differ across setups are not reported. Training-schedule effects on the law are not tested.

missing.what: Downstream accuracy across the four N sizes at fixed E and K. This is the only evidence in the study on whether downstream performance improves with scale.
On the stress test, the core law (0.27880) is less accurate than the Chinchilla and ATLAS baselines (0.233–0.236). High-reuse languages account for 95.4% of squared error.
Weighted R² for each law: about 0.99 on in-grid holdouts, falling to 0.55–0.87 on the larger model.
Transfer without refitting to changed language mixtures: RMSE 0.02649 versus 0.10246 for the best baseline.
ATLAS fitted with active N versus stored P parameters, and baselines with original versus per-language inputs, show that parameter and token counting changes fit quality.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source. It works in a narrow range: N from 93M to 590M, a stress test about 2x beyond that, and one seed per grid configuration. Its laws are judged by prediction RMSE; fitted exponents are not reported, so V7 evidence concerns prediction quality, not exponent disagreement. Rows r3 and r6 duplicate the same 0.17298 value. Allocation results concern active versus expert capacity and were moved off V3. The V6 verdicts rest on Table 21, not on extracted rows.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests a joint power-law-style loss model in multilingual decoder-only MoEs, not the original single-variable dense-model laws across the full parameter, token, and compute ranges.
Extrapolation is evaluated on held-out axes of the study's grid and one larger-model stress test, not on orders-of-magnitude extrapolation across general-purpose dense models.

The study evaluates expert-versus-active-parameter choices under total-parameter budgets; it does not establish separate stable power-law growth rates for optimal parameter and token counts over a broad compute range.
No comparison holds parameter count fixed while varying depth, width, or other architecture details.
It tests repeated-data effects in multilingual text pretraining only; it does not test image or video modalities, fine-tuning, or transfer.
Downstream benchmarks are evaluated across the studied configurations, but the paper does not fit or validate a general mapping from pretraining loss to downstream performance.

The paper compares several law formulations, parameterizations, and evaluation settings, but does not systematically vary every possible parameter-counting, data, training-schedule, or fitting-method choice.

statements.problem: RMSE 0.17298 is correct, but concentration of the selected law's remaining errors in high-repetition languages is not demonstrated. The explicit concentration diagnostic concerns the composition-aware extension. This short extrapolation also does not establish a challenge to orders-of-magnitude forecasting.
